To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“The transmissibility and the pathogenicity of disease-associated protein aggregates can vary greatly, and the latter depends strongly on the host response to the aggregate.”

the transmissibility of disease-associated protein aggregates in vivo is a complex function of the inoculum, host species and route, and that the pathological consequences of propagation in the recipient are a function of the inoculation dose and the host response to the aggregates.

the prion-like spreading of protein aggregates can be a major factor in the pathogenesis of a variety of human diseases, and that the transmissibility and pathogenicity of these aggregates are not always correlated.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) How do disease-associated protein aggregates propagate in vivo, and what are the consequences for the host?
understanding the molecular and cellular processes that underlie the propagation of disease-associated protein aggregates in vivo.

understanding the nature of protein misfolding and aggregation, the mechanisms by which misfolded proteins propagate, the factors that influence their transmissibility between hosts, and the pathological consequences, if any, of such propagation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, while there is no evidence that human-to-human transmission is possible in the absence of iatrogenic procedures, there is a real, albeit small risk of transmission by such means, and this risk is likely to increase as the population ages.
the transmissibility of disease-associated protein aggregates is a function of both their inherent properties and their interactions with the host.

, while the risk of iatrogenic transmission of prion diseases is well established, there is currently no convincing evidence for human-to-human transmissible disease propagation of other protein misfolding pathologies, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, Huntington’s disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and frontotemporal lobar degeneration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, while we cannot yet rule out the possibility of human-to-human transmissibility of disease-associated protein aggregates, we have shown that the risk is likely to be low.

the prion-like propagation of specific protein aggregates can occur in vivo, but the transmissibilities of such protein aggregates, as well as their pathogenicity, vary dramatically among different protein aggregates, host species, and routes of inoculation.

, while the transmissibilities of many disease-associated aggregates are likely to be much less than that of the prototypical prion, the pathogenicities of these aggregates may be more comparable to that of the prototypic prion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the absence of a clear understanding of how a disease-associated protein aggregates propagate in a new host, we cannot be confident about whether or not they are transmissible.

, although there may be a risk of transmission of some disease-associated protein aggregates between humans, the actual risks may not be as high as many fear, especially for diseases that are common in the population.
, although it is possible that some disease-associated aggregates can propagate in humans and cause disease, there is no evidence that they have done so, and the risk is likely to be very small.
